title: How long does it take for Suboxone® to kick in?
summary: Discover how long it takes for Suboxone to take effect and learn about common wait times, withdrawal symptoms, and proper administration.
body_markdown:
Most people feel the first effects of Suboxone® within about 20-60 minutes of the first dose, with the strongest effect at roughly 100 minutes. But timing is only half the question. When you take that first dose matters as much as how fast it works, and so does how much you take, because taking it too soon or at too high a first dose can trigger a reaction called precipitated withdrawal.


Below, we cover how fast it works, how long to wait before your first dose, and what to know in the days and weeks after you start.


Key takeaways


-


**Suboxone usually starts working in about 20–60 minutes,** and reaches peak effect around 100 minutes (roughly one hour and 40 minutes).


-


**You need to be in mild withdrawal before your first dose,** usually 12–24 hours after your last opioid use, and longer for fentanyl or long-acting opioids.


-


**Taking it too early can cause precipitated withdrawal,** which is why timing should be planned with a clinician.


-


**Because buprenorphine has a long half-life, using other opioids on top of Suboxone is largely blocked and dangerous.** There is no "safe" window to use again.


[Suboxone®](https://ophelia.com/blog/what-is-suboxone) , a common brand of buprenorphine/naloxone, is a partial opioid used in medication-assisted treatment (MAT) for opioid use disorder (OUD) to help relieve cravings and withdrawal symptoms without producing any euphoric effects once the stable dose is reached ([important safety information](https://ophelia.com/suboxone-safety) ). This way, you can feel mentally and physically well and remain clear-headed all day. It also lowers the chances of relapse and reduces the chances of overdose death by[70-80% as long as you keep taking it](https://www.optum.com/content/dam/optum3/optum/en/resources/PDFs/optumlabs-matforoudstudy-articl.pdf) .


## **How fast does Suboxone work?**


Suboxone starts working quickly. After your first dose dissolves, most people begin to feel relief from withdrawal within 20-60 minutes, and the medication reaches its[maximum effect at around 100 minutes](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2021/022410s042lbl.pdf) , about one hour and 40 minutes. Those effects then hold steady for many hours.


What you feel is subtle by design. Once you reach a stable dose,[buprenorphine](https://ophelia.com/blog/what-is-buprenorphine) quiets cravings and withdrawal without a “high” and without making you foggy, so you can feel like yourself and get through your day clear-headed.


### Does the film or tablet work faster?


Both[sublingual films and tablets](https://ophelia.com/blog/how-to-take-suboxone) dissolve under the tongue, and both are effective. Tablets can take a little longer to dissolve than films, so the form you're prescribed can slightly change how quickly you feel a dose. The difference is small, and the right form is the one you and your clinician choose together. Letting a dose fully dissolve, rather than chewing or swallowing it, affects how well it works more than film versus tablet does.


### How long should you wait before your first dose of Suboxone?


This is where timing gets important. You need to be in moderate withdrawal before your first dose so buprenorphine can attach to your opioid receptors cleanly. Most people[wait 12-24 hours after their last opioid use](https://www.drugs.com/medical-answers/long-you-wait-before-taking-suboxone-3557485/) , but the exact window depends on which opioid you were using.


### Wait times by opioid type


The right wait time depends on the opioid, some clear the body in hours, others take a day or more. Short-acting opioids clear faster, so the window is shorter; long-acting ones and fentanyl need more time, since they can linger longer than most people expect.


Opioid type Typical wait before first dose Examples


Short-acting opioids About 12–16 hours Heroin, oxycodone-type painkillers


Long-acting opioids About 17–48 hours Methadone, extended-release formulations


Fentanyl Often longer than expected Fentanyl can linger in the body, so your clinician may extend the wait and add medications in the meantime


Use these ranges as a starting point, not a rule. What you actually need can shift based on your dose, how long you've been using, and how you're feeling, that's what your care team confirms before the first dose.


### Why timing matters: avoiding precipitated withdrawal


If you take Suboxone while enough other opioids are still in your system, buprenorphine can push them off your receptors all at once and trigger precipitated withdrawal, a sudden, intense wave of withdrawal that is worse than what you would feel otherwise. Waiting until you're in moderate withdrawal is what prevents it.


[Common opioid withdrawal symptoms](https://ophelia.com/blog/what-to-expect-from-opioid-withdrawal) to watch for while you wait include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal cramps, fever or sweating, anxiety, insomnia, and muscle aches, pain, and spasms. When you go through this with support, your clinician can prescribe comfort medications and check in frequently to keep you as comfortable as possible.


## How long after taking Suboxone can you use opioids again?


People often ask this one quietly, so here's a direct answer. Once buprenorphine is in your system, it binds tightly to your opioid receptors and stays there far longer than most opioids, with effects that can last a day or more from a single dose. That means other opioids are largely **blocked** . They won't produce the effect you'd expect, and trying to override that by using more is how[overdoses](https://ophelia.com/blog/what-happens-when-you-overdose) happen, especially with fentanyl.


So there is no waiting period that makes using “safe” again. If you're thinking about using it, that isn't a failure. It's a signal to reach out to your care team. Adjusting your dose, adding support, and talking through cravings is what keeps treatment working.[Managing other substances](https://ophelia.com/blog/managing-other-substances-while-on-suboxone) while on Suboxone is a conversation your clinician has all the time, and it's always better to have it before, not after.


### Suboxone treatment over time


Research shows that Suboxone[is safe and effective as a long-term maintenance treatment](https://www.drugs.com/dosage/suboxone-film.html) . There is currently no maximum recommendation for the length of treatment, so you can continue as long as you and your care team believe the medication is helping.. Over time, patients tend to maintain these benefits even with lower doses. That said, everyone is different and, once stabilized, should discuss the length of their Suboxone treatment plan with healthcare professionals. Buprenorphine has a longer half-life than opioids like heroin or fentanyl, so it stays in your system for days instead of hours. That's why Suboxone can be taken once a day, twice a day, or for some people every other day, the medication is still active in your body between doses.


As with any treatment program, Suboxone should be prescribed as part of a comprehensive approach that also offers the opportunity for therapy, peer support, and community support groups if one finds it beneficial to talk about their experience with opioid drug use, recovery, and treatment. Prefer something more private than an inpatient treatment option? Ophelia’s got you covered. Our[telehealth model](https://ophelia.com/how-it-works) gives you access to your care team on your terms.

Before your first dose, your care team will ask what opioid you've been using, whether that's fentanyl, heroin, oxycodone, methadone, or something else, and use that to plan when to start Suboxone safely. They'll also outline what other medications you can take to stay comfortable while you wait, and what symptoms to watch for.

## Frequently asked questions


**How long after taking Suboxone should I feel better?**


You'll usually feel your first dose ease withdrawal within about an hour. Feeling fully steady takes longer. Over the first few days to a couple of weeks, you and your clinician fine-tune your dose until cravings and withdrawal are well managed. If a dose isn't holding you, tell your care team.


**What not to do before taking Suboxone?**


Don't take your first dose too early, before you're in moderate withdrawal, since that's the main cause of precipitated withdrawal. Don't underreport recent opioid use to your clinician, because accurate timing keeps you safe. And don't mix Suboxone with alcohol or benzodiazepines. When in doubt, ask your care team before that first dose.


**How long does a dose of Suboxone last?**


Because buprenorphine has a long half-life, a single dose can keep working for 24 hours or more, which is why most people take Suboxone once a day. Some people are prescribed split or every-other-day dosing. Your clinician decides what fits you.


**Is it normal to still feel some withdrawal after my first dose?**


Yes, especially early on. The first days are about finding your stable dose, so mild lingering symptoms can mean the dose isn't dialed in yet, not that Suboxone isn't working. Report what you're feeling to your care team so they can adjust rather than leaving you to wait it out.


**Where can I get Suboxone?**


Suboxone is a prescription medication, so you need a licensed clinician to prescribe it. That can happen in person at a clinic, or online through a telehealth program like Ophelia in states where we're licensed. If you're not sure whether you're eligible, you can check availability in your state before starting.
